questions.q: How many complex numbers z satisfy z² = z̄ (the conjugate of z)?
questions.x: Taking moduli, |z|² = |z|, so |z| = 0 or 1. z = 0 works; if |z| = 1 then z̄ = 1/z, so z³ = 1, giving z = 1, ω or ω². In all 4 solutions: 0, 1, ω, ω². Forgetting z = 0 gives 3.

questions.q: Which of these relations on R is a function whose inverse relation is also a function?
questions.x: y = x³ is one-one and onto R, so its inverse y = ∛x is again a function. y = x² and y = |x| are not one-one (x = 2 and x = −2 give the same y), and y² = x is not a function at all (x = 4 gives y = ±2).

questions.q: Which statement about the function f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x|x|, is true?
o: f is one-one but not onto
f is onto but not one-one
f is neither one-one nor onto
questions.x: f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 and −x² for x < 0, so f is strictly increasing (one-one) and reaches every real y (√y for y ≥ 0, −√(−y) for y < 0): it is a bijection. Compare x², which is neither.

questions.q: f(x) = (k cos x)/(π − 2x) for x ≠ π/2, and f(π/2) = 3. If f is continuous at x = π/2, what is k?
questions.x: Put t = π/2 − x: cos x = sin t and π − 2x = 2t, so the limit is k·(sin t)/(2t) → k/2. Continuity needs k/2 = 3, so k = 6. Forgetting the 2 in 2t gives 3.

questions.q: A father is three times as old as his son. In 10 years he will be twice as old as his son. How old is the son now?
questions.x: f = 3s and f + 10 = 2(s + 10). Substituting gives 3s + 10 = 2s + 20, so s = 10 (and the father is 30). Check: in 10 years 40 = 2 × 20.

questions.q: The homogeneous system x + 2y − z = 0, 2x + y + z = 0 has non-trivial solutions. In which ratio are x, y and z?
questions.x: The second equation minus twice the first gives −3y + 3z = 0, so z = y; then x + 2y − y = 0 gives x = −y. The solutions are (−t, t, t), i.e. x : y : z = 1 : −1 : −1. Check (1, −1, −1): 1 − 2 + 1 = 0 and 2 − 1 − 1 = 0.

questions.q: Real numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 3 and x² + xy + y² = 7. What is the value of x³ + y³?
questions.x: x² + xy + y² = (x + y)² − xy, so 9 − xy = 7 and xy = 2. Then x³ + y³ = (x + y)³ − 3xy(x + y) = 27 − 18 = 9. Check: the solutions are (1, 2) and (2, 1), and 1 + 8 = 9.

questions.q: Which of these is a factor of x³ + 3x² − x − 3?
questions.x: By the factor theorem, test x = −3: −27 + 27 + 3 − 3 = 0, so x + 3 is a factor. Grouping confirms it: x²(x + 3) − (x + 3) = (x + 3)(x − 1)(x + 1). Testing x = 3 gives 48, not 0.

questions.q: What is the sum of all two-digit numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 4?
questions.x: The numbers are 13, 17, …, 97, an A.P. with d = 4 and n = (97 − 13)/4 + 1 = 22 terms. Sum = 22 × (13 + 97)/2 = 11 × 110 = 1210. Forgetting the +1 in the count gives 21 terms and 1155.

questions.q: A culture starts with 500 bacteria, and the number doubles every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 2 hours?
questions.x: 2 hours is 6 periods of 20 minutes, so the count is 500 × 2⁶ = 500 × 64 = 32000. These counts form a G.P. 500, 1000, 2000, …, and after 6 doublings it is the 7th term. Using 2⁷ gives 64000.

questions.q: Four-digit numbers are formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with no digit repeated. How many of them are divisible by 5?
questions.x: A number divisible by 5 must end in 5 here (there is no 0). The other three places are filled from the remaining 5 digits: P(5, 3) = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60. 360 is the count of all such four-digit numbers.

questions.q: Using the first two terms of the binomial series, ∛65 is approximately:
questions.x: ∛65 = 4(1 + 1/64)^(1/3) ≈ 4(1 + 1/192) = 4 + 1/48 ≈ 4.0208. Forgetting to multiply 1/192 by 4 gives 4.0052; using the power ½ instead of ⅓ gives 4.0313.

questions.q: In two circles, arcs of the same length subtend angles of 60° and 75° at their centres. What is the ratio of the radius of the first circle to that of the second?
questions.x: Equal arcs give r₁θ₁ = r₂θ₂, so r₁/r₂ = θ₂/θ₁ = 75/60 = 5/4. The radius is larger where the angle is smaller; 4 : 5 is the ratio of the angles, not the radii.

questions.q: What is the value of sin 20° sin 40° sin 80°?
questions.x: sin 40° sin 80° = ½(cos 40° − cos 120°) = ½ cos 40° + ¼. Then sin 20° × that = ¼(sin 60° − sin 20°) + ¼ sin 20° = ¼ sin 60° = √3/8. 1/8 is the value of the cosine product cos 20° cos 40° cos 80°.

questions.q: What is the smallest positive period of f(x) = sin(πx) + cos(πx/2)?
questions.x: sin(πx) has period 2π/π = 2 and cos(πx/2) has period 2π/(π/2) = 4. The smallest common period is 4. 2 fails because cos(π(x + 2)/2) = −cos(πx/2). 4π comes from wrongly treating π as part of the period.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, C = 90°, a = 5 and b = 5√3. What are the hypotenuse c and the angle A?
questions.x: c = √(25 + 75) = 10 and tan A = a/b = 5/(5√3) = 1/√3, so A = 30° (and B = 60°). A = 60° is the angle opposite the longer leg b.

questions.q: In triangle ABC with area Δ and s = (a + b + c)/2, the radius r₁ of the escribed circle opposite A is:
questions.x: The escribed circle opposite A touches side a and the extensions of b and c, and r₁ = Δ/(s − a). Δ/s is the inradius r, Δ/(s − b) is r₂ and abc/(4Δ) is the circumradius R. For the 3-4-5 triangle, r₁ = 6/3 = 2.

questions.q: The general solution of cot θ = −1 is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: cot θ = −1 means tan θ = −1, whose principal solution is −π/4, and tan has period π, so θ = nπ − π/4 (this includes 3π/4 and 7π/4). The 2nπ forms each keep only one of these two families.

questions.q: On which interval is f(x) = x³ − 3x decreasing?
questions.x: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), which is negative exactly when −1 < x < 1. (−√3, √3) comes from the zeros of f itself, which say nothing about its slope.

questions.q: f is differentiable at x = a. What is the value of lim(h→0) [f(a + h²) − f(a)]/h?
questions.x: Write the quotient as {[f(a + h²) − f(a)]/h²} × h. The bracket tends to f′(a) (put k = h² → 0) and the factor h tends to 0, so the limit is f′(a) × 0 = 0.

questions.q: ∫₀^π x sin x dx equals:
questions.x: By parts, ∫x sin x dx = −x cos x + sin x. From 0 to π: (−π cos π + sin π) − 0 = π. The value 2 is ∫₀^π sin x dx without the factor x.

questions.q: The area of the region bounded by the curve y = eˣ, the y-axis and the line y = e is:
questions.x: The line y = e meets the curve at x = 1, and the line is above the curve for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, so the area is ∫₀¹ (e − eˣ) dx = e − (e − 1) = 1. The value e − 1 is the area under the curve instead. Check: ∫₁ᵉ ln y dy = 1.

questions.q: ∫ x tan⁻¹x dx equals:
o: x tan⁻¹x − ½ ln(1 + x²) + C
questions.x: Parts with u = tan⁻¹x, v = x²/2: (x²/2)tan⁻¹x − ½∫x²/(1 + x²) dx = (x²/2)tan⁻¹x − ½(x − tan⁻¹x) + C = ½(x² + 1)tan⁻¹x − x/2 + C. The last option is ∫tan⁻¹x dx.

questions.q: Two lines through the origin are perpendicular, and one of them is 2x + 3y = 0. What is their joint equation?
questions.x: The other line is 3x − 2y = 0. (2x + 3y)(3x − 2y) = 6x² − 4xy + 9xy − 6y² = 6x² + 5xy − 6y² = 0, and a + b = 0 confirms the lines are perpendicular.

questions.q: A triangle has one vertex at (1, 1), and the opposite side, of length 5, lies on the line 3x + 4y − 17 = 0. What is the area of the triangle?
questions.x: The height is the distance from (1, 1) to the line: |3 + 4 − 17|/5 = 2. Area = ½ × 5 × 2 = 5. Forgetting the ½ gives 10.

questions.q: Which point lies in the region given by x + y ≥ 3, x − y ≤ 1 and y ≤ 4?
questions.x: (2, 2): 4 ≥ 3, 0 ≤ 1 and 2 ≤ 4 are all true. (1, 1) fails x + y ≥ 3, (4, 1) fails x − y ≤ 1 and (1, 5) fails y ≤ 4.

questions.q: The line y = x/2 meets the ellipse x²/4 + y² = 1 at two points. What is the length of the chord joining them?
questions.x: Substitute y = x/2: x²/4 + x²/4 = 1, so x = ±√2 and y = ±1/√2. Chord length = √((2√2)² + (√2)²) = √(8 + 2) = √10.

questions.q: What is the eccentricity of a rectangular (equilateral) hyperbola?
questions.x: For a rectangular hyperbola a = b, so c² = a² + b² = 2a² and e = c/a = √2. Eccentricity 1 belongs to a parabola.

questions.q: A = (1, 2, 3) and B = (4, −1, 6). What is the point that divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 1?
questions.x: P = (1·A + 2·B)/3 = ((1 + 8)/3, (2 − 2)/3, (3 + 12)/3) = (3, 0, 5). Swapping the weights gives (2, 1, 4), the 1 : 2 point; (7, −4, 9) is the external point.

questions.q: A particle has velocity v = 2t + 3 m/s. How far does it travel during the third second, from t = 2 s to t = 3 s?
questions.x: v > 0 throughout, so distance = ∫₂³ (2t + 3) dt = [t² + 3t]₂³ = 18 − 10 = 8 m. 18 m is the distance in the first three seconds and 9 is v(3).

questions.q: A tap delivers water at 36 litres per minute. In SI units this flow rate is:
questions.x: 36 L = 36 × 10⁻³ m³ = 3.6 × 10⁻² m³, and 1 min = 60 s, so the rate is 3.6 × 10⁻²/60 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ m³ s⁻¹. Treating a litre as 1 m³ gives 6 × 10⁻¹; taking 1 L = 10⁻⁶ m³ (a cm³) gives 6 × 10⁻⁷; multiplying by 60 gives 2.16.

questions.q: A force F = (4î + 3ĵ) N acts on a body moving with velocity v = (2î − ĵ) m s⁻¹. The power delivered by the force, P = F · v, is:
questions.x: F · v = (4)(2) + (3)(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5 W. Ignoring the minus sign gives 11 W; multiplying the magnitudes 5 × √5 assumes the vectors are parallel.

questions.q: A car braking with a constant deceleration stops in a time t from a speed v. With the same deceleration, the time it takes to stop from a speed 2v is:
questions.x: From v = u + at with final speed zero, t = u/a, so the stopping time is proportional to the initial speed: 2t. The stopping distance (∝ u²) would become four times, which gives the tempting 4t.

questions.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 10 m s⁻¹ in 2 s, moves at 10 m s⁻¹ for 4 s, then slows uniformly to rest in 4 s. Its average velocity over the 10 s is:
questions.x: Displacement = area under the v–t graph = ½(10)(2) + 10 × 4 + ½(10)(4) = 10 + 40 + 20 = 70 m; check as a trapezium: ½(4 + 10) × 10 = 70 m. Average velocity = 70/10 = 7 m s⁻¹. Averaging 0 and 10 m s⁻¹ gives 5 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A 0.1 kg ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹ and, because of air resistance, rises only 15 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the energy lost to air resistance during the rise is:
questions.x: Initial KE = ½ × 0.1 × 20² = 20 J; PE at the top = 0.1 × 10 × 15 = 15 J; energy lost = 20 − 15 = 5 J. 20 J and 15 J are the two energies themselves, not their difference.

questions.q: A 2 kg book is lifted onto a shelf 3 m above the floor. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its gain in gravitational potential energy is:
questions.x: ΔPE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J. Leaving out g gives 6 J; halving as if it were kinetic energy gives 30 J.

questions.q: A 0.2 kg ball tied to a string moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at a speed of 3 m s⁻¹. Its angular momentum about the centre is:
questions.x: L = mvr = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.3 kg m² s⁻¹ (check: I = mr² = 0.05 kg m², ω = v/r = 6 rad s⁻¹, Iω = 0.3). Dividing by r instead of multiplying gives 1.2.

questions.q: A ship sails from a fresh-water river into the sea, where the water is denser. Its load is unchanged. The ship:
o: Rises a little, because a smaller volume of the denser water gives the same upthrust
Sinks a little, because sea water is denser
Floats at exactly the same level, because its weight has not changed
Rises a little, because the upthrust in sea water becomes greater than its weight
questions.x: Floating, upthrust = weight in both waters. Upthrust = ρVg, so with a larger ρ a smaller submerged volume V is needed: the ship rises a little. At rest the upthrust still equals the weight, not more.

questions.q: A particle performs SHM of amplitude 3 cm and period 2 s. What total distance does it travel in 5 s?
questions.x: 5 s is 2.5 periods. In each full period it travels 4 × amplitude = 12 cm, and in any half period 2 × amplitude, so the distance = 2 × 12 + 6 = 30 cm. Counting only 2 × amplitude per period gives 15 cm.

questions.q: Mechanical transverse waves cannot travel through:
questions.x: A transverse wave needs the medium to resist sideways (shear) displacement. A gas has no such rigidity, so only longitudinal waves travel through it. Strings, solids and water surfaces can carry transverse waves.

questions.q: Doctors use the Doppler effect with ultrasound to measure the:
o: Speed of blood flowing in an artery
questions.x: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood cells comes back with a shifted frequency, and the size of the shift gives the speed of the blood flow. Electrical activity of the heart is recorded by an ECG, not by ultrasound.

questions.q: In a beam of plane-polarised light, the vibrations of the electric field are:
o: In all directions at right angles to the direction of travel
Confined to one plane that contains the direction of travel
Absent, because a polaroid has removed them
questions.x: Plane-polarised light has its electric field vibrating in a single plane that contains the direction of propagation. Vibrations in all perpendicular directions describe unpolarised light.

questions.q: An advantage of an optical fibre over a copper cable for carrying telephone signals is that the fibre:
o: Can also carry electric power to the telephone
Is not affected by electrical interference from nearby circuits
Makes light travel faster than it does in air
Never needs any repeaters, however long it is
questions.x: Signals in a fibre are light, so nearby electric and magnetic fields do not disturb them; fibres also carry far more information with less loss. Light is slower in glass than in air, and long links still need repeaters.

questions.q: Air rushing out of a punctured tyre feels cool. The best explanation is that the air:
o: Gives its heat to the tyre rubber
Is compressed as it leaves the valve
Takes in heat from the surroundings as it expands
Expands almost adiabatically and does work using its own internal energy
questions.x: The expansion is fast, so there is little time for heat exchange (nearly adiabatic). The gas does work pushing back the outside air, and with Q ≈ 0 this comes from its internal energy, so its temperature falls.

questions.q: Two Carnot engines work in series: the first between 600 K and 400 K, and the second takes all the heat rejected by the first and works between 400 K and 300 K. The overall efficiency of the pair is:
questions.x: Take 600 J from the source: engine 1 (η = 1/3) does 200 J and rejects 400 J; engine 2 (η = 1/4) does 100 J and rejects 300 J. Total work 300 J out of 600 J = 50%, the same as one Carnot engine from 600 K to 300 K. Adding 33% and 25% gives 58%.

questions.q: A flat surface is placed in a uniform electric field with its plane parallel to the field lines. The electric flux through it is:
questions.x: Φ = EA cos θ, where θ is between the field and the normal to the surface. With the plane parallel to the field, θ = 90° and Φ = 0: no lines pass through.

questions.q: A dust particle of mass 2 mg carries a charge of +4 μC. It floats at rest in a uniform vertical electric field. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the field is:
questions.x: Balance: qE = mg, so E = (2 × 10⁻⁶ kg × 10)/(4 × 10⁻⁶ C) = 5 N C⁻¹. The force on a positive charge is along the field, and it must point up to balance the weight. Taking 2 mg as 2 × 10⁻⁵ kg gives 50 N C⁻¹.

questions.q: To measure a current with a potentiometer, the current is passed through a standard 2 Ω resistor and the p.d. across that resistor is balanced by 40 cm of potentiometer wire. The potential gradient of the wire is 0.01 V cm⁻¹. The current is:
questions.x: V = 0.01 V cm⁻¹ × 40 cm = 0.4 V, so I = V/R = 0.4/2 = 0.2 A. Multiplying by R instead of dividing gives 0.8 A.

questions.q: An electric iron rated 500 W is used for 10 minutes. The electrical energy it uses is:
questions.x: E = Pt = 500 W × (10 × 60) s = 3 × 10⁵ J. Leaving the time in minutes gives 5 × 10³ J.

questions.q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry currents of 5 A each in opposite directions. The magnetic field at the point midway between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
questions.x: Each wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5 / 0.05 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at the midpoint. With opposite currents the two fields there point the same way, so they add to 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. Zero would be the answer for currents in the same direction.

questions.q: An aircraft with a wingspan of 20 m flies horizontally at 250 m s⁻¹ where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. The emf induced between its wing tips is:
questions.x: The horizontal wings cut the vertical field component: ε = BLv = 4 × 10⁻⁵ × 20 × 250 = 0.2 V. A slip in the power of ten gives 2 V or 0.02 V.

questions.q: In a simple DC generator, the output current is made to flow in one direction in the external circuit by:
questions.x: The split rings reverse the coil's connections to the brushes every half turn, just when the coil's emf reverses, so the external current keeps one direction. Slip rings give an AC output.

questions.q: An inductor of 0.1 H with negligible resistance has a reactance of 31.4 Ω. The frequency of the supply is (π ≈ 3.14):
questions.x: XL = 2πfL, so f = XL/(2πL) = 31.4/(2 × 3.14 × 0.1) = 31.4/0.628 = 50 Hz. Forgetting the 2π gives 314 Hz; forgetting just the 2 gives 100 Hz.

questions.q: A steel wire (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) has a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm². What load will produce a tensile strain of 0.1% in it?
questions.x: Strain = 0.1% = 1 × 10⁻³, so stress = Y × strain = 2 × 10⁸ Pa, and F = stress × A = 2 × 10⁸ × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 100 N. Taking 0.1% as 0.01 gives 1000 N; taking it as 0.1 gives 1 × 10⁵ N.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier is connected to the 50 Hz mains. The time from the start of one output pulse to the start of the next is:
questions.x: One input cycle lasts 1/50 s = 20 ms, and a full-wave rectifier gives two output pulses per cycle, so one pulse starts every 10 ms (100 pulses per second). 20 ms is the spacing for a half-wave rectifier.

questions.q: The Compton shift is easy to observe with X-rays but practically impossible to see with visible light. The reason is that:
o: Visible light photons are not scattered by electrons at all
The shift is much smaller for long wavelengths
The shift, at most a few picometres, is a tiny fraction of a visible wavelength of about 500 nm
questions.x: Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) is at most about 5 × 10⁻¹² m whatever the wavelength. For X-rays of about 10⁻¹¹ m this is a large fraction, but for 5 × 10⁻⁷ m light it is only about 1 part in 10⁵. The shift does not depend on the wavelength, and visible photons do have momentum h/λ.

questions.q: The fastest photoelectrons emitted from a metal have a kinetic energy of 2 eV. The stopping potential needed to stop all of them is:
questions.x: The stopping potential V₀ satisfies eV₀ = K.E.max, so a K.E.max of 2 eV needs V₀ = 2 V. Writing 2 eV as 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and dropping the power of ten gives 3.2 V; halving or doubling the energy has no basis, since 1 eV is exactly the energy one electron gains through 1 V.

questions.q: Bohr's model of the atom gives correct values for the spectral lines of:
o: All atoms, including those with many electrons
Hydrogen and other ions with a single electron
Only atoms with completely filled shells
Only heavy atoms such as uranium
questions.x: Bohr's theory works for hydrogen and one-electron ions such as He⁺, but it cannot explain the spectra of atoms with two or more electrons, whose electrons interact with each other.

questions.q: Tritium, ³₁H, is an isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus contains:
questions.x: Z = 1 gives 1 proton, and A − Z = 3 − 1 = 2 neutrons. Taking A as the number of neutrons gives 3 neutrons; every isotope of hydrogen has exactly 1 proton.

questions.q: Astronomers on the Earth see distant galaxies moving away in every direction, faster the farther away they are. This means that:
o: The Earth is at the centre of the expansion
The galaxies are moving through a fixed space away from our Galaxy only
Observers in any galaxy would see the same pattern, so the Earth is not at a centre
Galaxies nearer to us must be moving faster
questions.x: In a uniform expansion (v = H₀d) every distance grows in the same proportion, so from any galaxy all others appear to recede with speed proportional to distance; there is no centre. Nearer galaxies recede more slowly, not faster.

questions.q: A 8.4 g mixture of magnesium carbonate and sodium chloride is heated strongly until no more gas is given off: MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂ (NaCl does not change). 1.12 dm³ of CO₂, measured at STP, is collected. The percentage by mass of MgCO₃ in the mixture is: (C = 12, O = 16, Mg = 24; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: CO₂ = 1.12/22.4 = 0.05 mol, so MgCO₃ = 0.05 mol = 0.05 × 84 = 4.2 g. Percentage = 4.2/8.4 × 100 = 50%. Using the mass of CO₂ (2.2 g) in place of MgCO₃ gives about 26%, close to the 25% option.

questions.q: During crystallisation, the hot saturated solution is filtered before it is left to cool. The purpose of this filtration is to:
questions.x: Insoluble impurities stay on the filter paper while the dissolved compound passes through; soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor after cooling. Thinking this step removes soluble impurities is the common slip.

questions.q: A sealed steel cylinder of gas is at 2.0 atm at 27 °C. If it is warmed to 57 °C, its pressure becomes:
questions.x: At constant volume, P ∝ T (in K): P₂ = 2.0 × 330/300 = 2.2 atm. Using °C (2.0 × 57/27) gives about 4.2 atm; inverting the ratio gives 1.8 atm.

questions.q: The lattice energy of MgO is about four times that of NaF, although the ions in the two crystals are of similar size. The main reason is that:
o: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are much larger than Na⁺ and F⁻
MgO is a covalent network solid
MgO has a higher molar mass than NaF
The charges on both ions are doubled (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻), and attraction depends on the product of the charges
questions.x: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ion charges and falls with the distance between them. With similar ionic radii, 2 × 2 = 4 compared with 1 × 1 = 1 gives about four times the lattice energy. Larger ions would lower it, not raise it.

questions.q: How many electrons in an atom can have the quantum numbers n = 3 and m = 0?
questions.x: For n = 3, l can be 0, 1 or 2; each has exactly one orbital with m = 0 (3s, one 3p, one 3d), so 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6. 3 counts orbitals instead of electrons, and 2 counts only the 3s orbital.

questions.q: The first four ionisation energies of element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10541 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?
questions.x: The big jump comes between the second and third ionisation energies, so X has two electrons in its outer shell and the third must come from an inner shell: X is in group 2 (the values are those of Mg). Group 1 is the slip of placing the jump after the first value.

questions.q: A molecule XCl₃ has a trigonal pyramidal shape, and X forms only single bonds and keeps an octet. In which group of the periodic table is X?
questions.x: A pyramidal AX₃ shape needs three bond pairs and one lone pair, i.e. 8 electrons around X. Three come from the Cl atoms, so X supplies 5 valence electrons and is in group 15 (as in NCl₃ or PCl₃). A group 13 atom gives a trigonal planar XCl₃ with no lone pair; a group 14 atom would be left with an unpaired electron.

questions.q: The hydration enthalpy of Li⁺ is much more negative than that of K⁺. The reason is that Li⁺:
o: Has a larger charge than K⁺
Is larger, so more water molecules fit around it
Is smaller, so its charge density is higher and it attracts water molecules more strongly
Has a lower ionisation energy than potassium
questions.x: Both ions carry +1 charge, but Li⁺ is much smaller, so the charge is concentrated and the ion–dipole attraction to water is stronger, releasing more energy. Li⁺ does not have a larger charge, and the ionisation energy of Li is in fact higher than that of K.

questions.q: Which change alters the numerical value of Kc for a given reversible reaction?
questions.x: Kc is constant at a fixed temperature. Adding reactant or changing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium, but the new concentrations still give the same Kc; a catalyst changes neither. Only a change of temperature changes Kc itself.

questions.q: Solid sodium ethanoate is dissolved in a solution of ethanoic acid. What happens to the ionisation of the acid and to the pH?
o: Ionisation increases and the pH falls
Ionisation is suppressed and the pH falls
Ionisation increases and the pH rises
Ionisation is suppressed and the pH rises
questions.x: CH₃COONa adds CH₃COO⁻, an ion common to CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺; the equilibrium shifts to the left, so [H⁺] falls and the pH rises. 'pH falls' links 'adding a salt of the acid' with more acidity, the tempting slip.

questions.q: Seawater and pure water are separated by a semipermeable membrane. A pressure greater than the osmotic pressure of seawater is applied on the seawater side. What happens?
o: Water passes from the pure water into the seawater
Water passes from the seawater into the pure water
Salt ions pass through into the pure water
No water moves across the membrane
questions.x: Applying more than the osmotic pressure reverses osmosis: solvent is pushed from the solution into the pure solvent, which is how seawater is desalinated. Without the extra pressure, water would move the other way (ordinary osmosis).

questions.q: Sodium metal cannot be obtained by electrolysing aqueous sodium chloride. The reason is that:
o: Na⁺ ions move to the anode instead of the cathode
Chloride ions are reduced before Na⁺ ions
Sodium chloride does not ionise in water
Water is reduced at the cathode far more easily than Na⁺, because E°(Na⁺/Na) is very negative
questions.x: E°(Na⁺/Na) = −2.71 V, far more negative than the reduction of water, so the cathode gives hydrogen, not sodium. That is why sodium is made from molten NaCl in the Downs cell.

questions.q: Which of these is a primary cell, that is, one that cannot be recharged?
questions.x: In the zinc–carbon dry cell the reactions cannot be reversed usefully, so it is thrown away when used up. The lead storage battery, the nickel–cadmium cell and the lithium-ion cell are secondary (rechargeable) cells.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the rate of most reactions is greatest at the start and falls as the reaction goes on. The main reason is that:
o: The rate constant decreases with time
The activation energy rises as products form
The concentrations of the reactants decrease
questions.x: Rate depends on reactant concentration; as reactants are used up there are fewer collisions per second, so the rate falls. The rate constant stays the same at a fixed temperature.

questions.q: Tellurium (atomic mass 127.6) is placed before iodine (atomic mass 126.9) in the periodic table, against the order of atomic masses. The modern periodic table justifies this because:
o: Iodine atoms have more neutrons than tellurium atoms
Atomic masses were measured wrongly in Mendeleev's time
Tellurium has the lower atomic number (52) and iodine the higher (53)
Tellurium is a metal and iodine is a non-metal
questions.x: The modern table is arranged by atomic number, and Te (52) comes before I (53); iodine also clearly belongs with the halogens. The atomic masses are correct: tellurium has heavier isotopes, so it has more neutrons, not fewer.

questions.q: Equal masses of magnesium and calcium are each added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the ratio of the volume of hydrogen from magnesium to that from calcium, measured under the same conditions? (Mg = 24, Ca = 40)
questions.x: Both react as M + 2HCl → MCl₂ + H₂, so moles of H₂ equal moles of metal. For mass m: m/24 : m/40 = 40 : 24 = 5 : 3. Inverting the ratio gives 3 : 5; equal masses are not equal moles, so 1 : 1 is wrong.

questions.q: Oleum, H₂S₂O₇, is diluted with water: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. What mass of H₂SO₄ is obtained from 17.8 g of oleum? (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.x: M(H₂S₂O₇) = 2 + 64 + 112 = 178 g mol⁻¹, so 0.10 mol gives 0.20 mol H₂SO₄ = 0.20 × 98 = 19.6 g. Mass check: 17.8 g oleum + 1.8 g water = 19.6 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 9.8 g.

questions.q: 10 dm³ of hydrogen and 15 dm³ of chlorine are exploded together: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What volume of HCl forms, and which gas is left over?
o: 20 dm³ HCl; 5 dm³ of Cl₂ left
10 dm³ HCl; 5 dm³ of Cl₂ left
20 dm³ HCl; 5 dm³ of H₂ left
questions.x: H₂ is limiting: 10 dm³ H₂ uses 10 dm³ Cl₂ and gives 2 × 10 = 20 dm³ HCl, leaving 15 − 10 = 5 dm³ Cl₂. Volume check: 20 + 5 = 25 dm³, unchanged as the equation has 2 volumes on each side. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 10 dm³ HCl.

questions.q: Most transition metals have much higher melting points than the s-block metals mainly because:
o: Both 3d and 4s electrons take part in metallic bonding, making it stronger
They form ionic lattices in the solid state
Their atoms are joined by hydrogen bonds
Their d subshells are always completely filled
questions.x: Transition metals contribute unpaired d electrons as well as s electrons to the sea of delocalised electrons, and their atoms are small, so the metallic bonding is strong. Metals are not ionic lattices, so that option is wrong.

questions.q: Propanone exists in equilibrium with a small amount of its enol form: CH₃COCH₃ ⇌ CH₂=C(OH)CH₃. This type of isomerism is called:
questions.x: Keto and enol forms differ by the movement of an H atom and a double bond and change into each other in a dynamic equilibrium; this is tautomerism. Metamerism involves different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional group, as in ethers.

questions.q: Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, is hydrogenated completely with excess H₂ over nickel. The product is then chlorinated in sunlight. How many structurally different monochloro products can form?
questions.x: Full hydrogenation gives propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃, which has two kinds of hydrogen (end CH₃ and middle CH₂), so 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane form. Answering 3 counts each carbon separately, ignoring that the two CH₃ groups are equivalent.

questions.q: One volume of a gaseous alkane needs exactly 6.5 volumes of oxygen for complete combustion, both measured at the same temperature and pressure. The alkane is:
questions.x: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n+1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n+1)H₂O, so (3n+1)/2 = 6.5 gives n = 4 (C₄H₁₀ + 6.5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O; O: 13 = 8 + 5). Propane needs 5 and pentane 8 volumes; forgetting that H₂O also uses oxygen gives n = 6.5, not a whole number.

questions.q: Nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution much more slowly than benzene. The reason is that the –NO₂ group:
o: Withdraws electron density from the ring, making it less attractive to electrophiles
Donates electron density to the ring through a lone pair
Is so large that it blocks every position of the ring
Reacts with the electrophile before the ring can
questions.x: –NO₂ pulls electrons out of the ring by both induction and resonance, lowering the electron density most at ortho and para, so the ring is deactivated and attack goes slowly to meta. Lone-pair donation describes activating groups such as –OH.

questions.q: Bromoethane can give either ethanol (substitution) or ethene (elimination) with KOH. Which conditions favour elimination?
o: Dilute aqueous KOH at room temperature
Dilute aqueous KOH, cooled in ice
questions.x: In ethanol, with a high concentration of base and heat, OH⁻ (and C₂H₅O⁻) acts as a base and removes a β-hydrogen, giving CH₂=CH₂. Aqueous, dilute, cool conditions favour OH⁻ acting as a nucleophile and give ethanol.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl. The organic product is:
questions.x: The O–H of phenol is acylated: C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCl → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl, an ester. Ethyl benzoate has the acid and alcohol parts the other way round; the C–O bond of phenol does not break, so chlorobenzene does not form.

questions.q: Which reagent distinguishes ethanal, CH₃CHO, from propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO?
questions.x: Ethanal has the CH₃CO– group and gives yellow iodoform; propanal does not. Both are aliphatic aldehydes, so both give a silver mirror, a red Fehling's precipitate and an orange 2,4-DNPH precipitate.

questions.q: 0.75 g of glycine (75 g mol⁻¹) reacts exactly with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid, each glycine taking up one H⁺. What volume of acid is needed?
questions.x: Moles of glycine = 0.75/75 = 0.010 mol, so 0.010 mol HCl is needed: 0.010/0.10 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³ (the COO⁻ of the zwitterion becomes COOH). Leaving the answer as 0.10 dm³ read as 10 cm³ is a units slip; assuming two H⁺ per glycine gives 200 cm³.

questions.q: Vegetable oils such as sunflower oil are liquids at room temperature, while animal fats such as beef fat are solids. The main reason is that the oils:
o: Contain more C=C double bonds in their fatty acid chains, so the molecules pack less closely
Contain more glycerol units per molecule
Have much higher molar masses than fats
Are made of free fatty acids rather than triglycerides
questions.x: Both are triglycerides of glycerol. The cis double bonds in unsaturated chains put bends in them, so the molecules cannot pack tightly and the van der Waals forces are weaker, giving a lower melting point. Every triglyceride has one glycerol unit, so that option is wrong.

questions.q: An infrared spectrum shows a sharp band near 2250 cm⁻¹. This is typical of which bond?
questions.x: Triple bonds such as C≡N absorb in the 2100–2260 cm⁻¹ region. C=O absorbs near 1700 cm⁻¹, O–H as a broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and C–H near 2850–3000 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: In a three-way catalytic converter, nitrogen monoxide, NO, from the engine is converted mainly into:
questions.x: On the Pt/Rh catalyst NO is reduced, for example 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂, so harmless nitrogen leaves the exhaust. NO₂ is the oxidised pollutant that forms from NO in the air; making it would worsen pollution.

questions.q: Which of the following is equal to (110110)₂?
questions.x: (110110)₂ = 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 54; grouping in threes, 110 110 gives (66)₈ = 6×8 + 6 = 54. (54)₈ is wrong because 54 is the decimal value, and in octal (54)₈ = 44.

questions.q: A 0 is added to the right end of an unsigned binary number, so (1011)₂ becomes (10110)₂. What happens to its value?
questions.x: Every bit moves one place left, so each place value is doubled: (1011)₂ = 11 becomes (10110)₂ = 22. Adding a 0 on the left, not the right, would leave the value unchanged.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches two protocols with the OSI layers at which they work?
o: HTTP: Session layer; TCP: Network layer
HTTP: Application layer; TCP: Transport layer
IP: Transport layer; TCP: Application layer
IP: Data Link layer; HTTP: Transport layer
questions.x: HTTP serves user programs at the Application layer, TCP gives end-to-end reliable delivery at the Transport layer, and IP routes packets at the Network layer. Putting TCP at the Network layer confuses it with IP.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a network with its type?
o: Computers in one school building: LAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: WAN
Computers in one school building: WAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: LAN
Computers in one school building: MAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: LAN
Computers in one school building: WAN; branches of a bank all over Pakistan: MAN
questions.x: One building is a small area, so it is a LAN; branches across the country cover a very large area, so they form a WAN. A MAN covers about one city, which is too large for one building and too small for a whole country.

questions.q: Which statement about the Internet and the World Wide Web is correct?
o: The Internet and the Web are two names for exactly the same thing
The Internet is one service that runs on the Web, like e-mail
The Web is the cables and routers, and the Internet is the web pages
The Web is one service that runs on the Internet; e-mail and FTP are other Internet services
questions.x: The Internet is the worldwide network of networks; the Web is the system of linked pages that uses it through HTTP, alongside services like e-mail and FTP. Treating the two words as the same thing is the common mistake.

questions.q: A team has built a speech-recognition app. What is the best way to find out whether it is biased?
o: Compare its error rates for different groups of speakers
Test it only on the developers' own voices
Measure only its overall accuracy on all recordings
Check how quickly it turns speech into text
questions.x: Bias shows up as different error rates for different groups, such as accents, ages or genders, so results must be compared group by group. A single overall accuracy can look good while one group gets far worse results.

questions.q: A program stores all of a user's different strong passwords in encrypted form, unlocked by one master password. Such a program is a:
questions.x: A password manager keeps many strong, unique passwords safely so the user need remember only one. A keylogger is malware that steals passwords rather than protecting them.

questions.q: Data from satellites and weather stations is fed into computer models that predict tomorrow's rain and temperature. This is the use of computers in:
questions.x: Weather forecasting runs large numbers of calculations on weather data to predict future conditions. Computer-aided manufacturing controls machines that make products.

questions.q: The company that owns the data centres and rents out servers, storage and software over the Internet is called a:
questions.x: A cloud service provider runs the data centres and sells cloud resources to customers. A hypervisor is software inside a server that runs virtual machines.

questions.q: When text or a file is cut or copied, Windows holds it in a temporary storage area until it is pasted. This area is the:
questions.x: The clipboard keeps the most recently cut or copied item in memory so that it can be pasted. The Recycle Bin holds deleted files, not copied ones.

questions.q: In a worksheet, columns are lettered A, B, C and so on. What is the letter of the column that comes right after column Z?
questions.x: After the 26 single letters, column names continue with two letters, starting at AA, then AB and so on. AZ comes 26 columns after Z, and Z1 is a cell address.

questions.q: Marks(Roll, Subject, Name, Score) has the key (Roll, Subject), with Roll → Name and (Roll, Subject) → Score. Which non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole key?
questions.x: Score needs both Roll and Subject to be known, so it depends on the whole key. Name depends on Roll alone, which is a partial dependency.

questions.q: In Student(RollNo, Name, City), RollNo is unique, but two students may have the same Name and City. Which set of columns is a super key but NOT a candidate key?
questions.x: {RollNo, Name} identifies every row because it contains RollNo, so it is a super key; it is not minimal, since RollNo alone already works, so it is not a candidate key. {RollNo} is a candidate key, and {Name, City} is not unique.

questions.q: A clerk enters data through ready-made forms and menus and never writes SQL or programs. What kind of database user is the clerk?
questions.x: End users work with the database through forms, menus and reports made for them. Application programmers write those programs, and the DBA manages security, backup and performance.

questions.q: A report on Student(Name, City) is grouped by City. There are 3 students from Lahore, 2 from Karachi and 1 from Multan. How many times is the City Header section printed?
questions.x: A group header is printed once at the start of each group, and there are 3 cities, so it prints 3 times. Printing once per student, 6 times, is what the Detail section does.

questions.q: Why must a C program be translated before the computer can run it?
o: The CPU can execute only assembly-language instructions
Translation is needed only to remove the comments
The CPU can execute only machine-language instructions
Translation is needed only to check the spelling of variables
questions.x: A processor understands only machine code (binary instructions), so C statements must be compiled into it. Assembly language also has to be translated, by an assembler.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 9 / 2.0 + 1);
```
questions.x: 9 / 2.0 = 4.5 because 2.0 is a floating-point constant, then 4.5 + 1 = 5.5. Integer division 9 / 2 = 4 would give 5.0.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", 3, 4);
```
questions.x: printf prints according to its format string, which has one %d, so it prints 3; the extra argument 4 is not used. It is not a compile error, though a compiler may warn about it.
Inside the function x * 2 = 5.4, but the return type is int, so the value is converted to int by dropping the fraction: 5. It is not rounded to 6, and %d could not print 5.4.

questions.q: Which task is easier to program with an `if-else-if` ladder than with a `switch` statement?
o: Choosing an action for a menu choice of 1, 2 or 3
Choosing an action for the operator characters `'+'`, `'-'` and `'*'`
Printing a day name for a day number from 1 to 7
Choosing a tax rate from the range in which a `float` salary lies
questions.x: A case label must be a single integer or character constant, so a switch cannot test ranges of a float value; an if-else-if ladder can (salary < 50000.0, and so on). The other tasks match one exact integer or character value each, which a switch does well.
isprime returns 1 only for 2, 3, 5 and 7 (1 is rejected by n < 2, and 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 have a divisor), so c = 4. 5 wrongly counts 1 as prime.

questions.q: Before the official release, a company lets a group of real users outside the company try a nearly finished app and report the problems they meet. This is:
questions.x: Beta testing is done by real users in their own setting just before release. Alpha testing is the earlier stage done inside the developer's own company, and unit testing checks single parts of the code.

questions.q: In a debugger, running a program one statement at a time to see what each line does is called:
questions.x: Stepping executes one line, then pauses so variables can be checked before the next line. Regression testing re-runs old tests after a change; it is not done line by line.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
print("abc" < "abd", "Z" < "a")
```
questions.x: Strings are compared character by character: "abc" and "abd" first differ at c < d, so True. Capital letters come before small letters in character codes (Z is 90, a is 97), so "Z" < "a" is also True.

questions.q: How many times does the body of `for i in range(3, 8):` run?
questions.x: `range(3, 8)` gives 3, 4, 5, 6, 7: the end value 8 is left out, so 5 passes. 6 wrongly counts 8 as well.

questions.q:
Assume `import tkinter as tk` and a working display. The user clicks Add three times. What does the label show then?
```
count = 0
def add():
    global count
    count += 1
    lbl.config(text=str(count))
root = tk.Tk()
lbl = tk.Label(root, text="0")
lbl.pack()
tk.Button(root, text="Add", command=add).pack()
root.mainloop()
```
questions.x: Each click calls `add`, which adds 1 to the global `count` and puts its new value in the label: 1, 2, then 3. `config` replaces the label's text, so it shows 3.

questions.q: Which statement about searching an unsorted list of 500 names is true?
o: Binary search works on it; linear search needs it sorted first
Both methods need the list sorted first
Linear search works on it; binary search needs it sorted first
Neither method can be used until it is sorted
questions.x: Linear search checks every element in turn, so the order does not matter. Binary search discards half the list after each comparison, which is valid only if the list is sorted.

questions.q: Rule: ∀x (E(x) → M(x)), where E(x) means "x is an engineer" and M(x) means "x knows maths". Fact: E(Sana). What can be concluded?
o: Every person who knows maths is an engineer
questions.x: The rule holds for every x, so it holds for Sana: E(Sana) → M(Sana). With E(Sana) true, modus ponens gives M(Sana). The rule does not say that everyone who knows maths is an engineer.

questions.q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
o: Students who sleep 8 hours score higher on average than students who sleep 5 hours
questions.x: A hypothesis is a statement that can be checked with data, here by comparing two groups' average scores. A question is not a hypothesis, and opinions such as "sleep is wonderful" cannot be measured.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis for a new food-delivery startup, which of these is a Strength?
o: Online ordering is growing fast in the city
A large company may start a cheaper service
Its founders have strong app-development skills
It has little money for advertising
questions.x: Strengths and weaknesses are internal to the business; the founders' skills are an internal advantage. Growing online ordering is an external Opportunity, a rival is a Threat and a small budget is a Weakness.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
o: To explain why wood leaves less ash than metal leaves powder
To criticise the chemists who believed in a hidden burning substance
To argue that a mistaken theory can help science when it is tested
To show that students should not study old theories at all
questions.x: The writer says "a good wrong theory can do as much to move knowledge forward as a right one" and uses the burning theory as the example. The chemists are not criticised: they took the theory "seriously enough to test".

questions.q: According to the passage, what did the old theory predict about a metal heated until it crumbled?
o: That it would leave only a little ash, as wood does
That the powder would weigh more than the metal
That the powder would weigh less than the metal
That it would take something from the air
questions.x: The prediction was that the powder "should, having lost something, weigh less". That it weighed more was the result that the workers actually found, the opposite of the prediction.

questions.q: The writer would most likely agree that a theory is most useful to science when it:
o: explains everything without needing to be checked
is accepted by most experts of its time
is correct from the very beginning
makes claims that experiments could show to be false
questions.x: The burning theory proved useful because it "made a prediction that could be checked", and the writer says the real failure is "refusing to find out whether you are wrong". Being correct from the start is not required: the useful theory here was wrong.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tidy" most nearly means:
o: neat and simple in its explanation
questions.x: "The theory was tidy, and it explained a great deal": it was neat and simple. "Clean and well swept" is the word's meaning for a room, not for a theory.

questions.q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards the old theory of burning?
o: Scornful, treating it as a foolish obstacle
Respectful of its usefulness even though it was wrong
Convinced that it was mostly correct
questions.x: The writer calls it "tidy", says it "explained a great deal" and credits it with opening "the way to a new understanding of chemistry". Scorn is wrong: the writer objects to treating wrong ideas "as if they had been nothing but obstacles".

questions.q: The main subject of the passage is:
o: food waste at large weddings and some practical ways of reducing it
why weddings should stop serving meals to guests
how careless and selfish hosts have become
how caterers cook for very large events
questions.x: The passage describes the waste and then the volunteers and smaller portions that tackle it, ending that a wedding "simply needs a plan". Blaming hosts is rejected: "It is easy to blame hosts, but"

questions.q: Why does the writer call "untouched" the key word?
o: Volunteers will not take any food that caterers have cooked
Only food that has not reached a guest's plate can safely be passed on
Shelters accept only food that has been frozen
Untouched food can be sold back to the caterers
questions.x: "Food that has sat on a guest's plate cannot be passed on", so the work depends on the surplus being set aside "before it is served". Volunteers in fact collect food from caterers.

questions.q: Following the reasoning of the second paragraph, which of these would most likely help change the custom?
o: One family ordering exactly enough food to set an example
Many families in a community agreeing together to order more modest amounts
Caterers raising the price of every dish
Guests being urged to eat larger meals
questions.x: The custom is kept alive by the fear of shame, and "No single family can change the custom alone", so a shared agreement would remove the shame of ordering less. One family acting alone is exactly what the writer says will not work.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "surplus" most nearly means:
o: the extra food beyond what is needed
the finest dishes of the meal
money left over after paying the caterers
questions.x: The "surplus" is the food left over when hosts "order far more than can be eaten", set aside "before it is served". The passage speaks of food here, not money.

questions.q: The writer's attitude towards the hosts is best described as:
o: full of praise for their generosity
understanding, seeing them as trapped by a custom
questions.x: The writer says hosts "are caught in a custom that punishes moderation" and explains the "shame of running out". Contempt is ruled out by "It is easy to blame hosts, but".
